title: Masei: every stop named (Numbers 33)
hookLine: forty-two stations of the journey listed, even the forgettable ones

cards: Scroll back far enough in the photos on your phone and you'll find the in-between places.
Not the wedding or the graduation, but a motel parking lot, a hospital vending machine, a borrowed apartment you lived in for three months. Some of them may have been hard stretches.
The last portion of the book of Numbers opens with a list that's easy to skim. It names every single place the people camped, from the night they left Egypt to the edge of the promised land.

teach.b: The portion is called Masei, which means the journeys of.

It begins, in paraphrase: these are the journeys of the children of Israel, who went out of Egypt, and Moses wrote down their starting points, stage by stage, at God's command. Then the list. Rameses.
Succoth. Etham. Marah, where the water was bitter.
Elim, with twelve springs and seventy palm trees. And on, place after place.

teach.h: FORTY-TWO STATIONS, MANY WITH NO STORY.
teach.b: Tradition counts forty-two stations in all. Some are well-known: Sinai, Kadesh. Others, like Rithmah and Rimmon-perez, come with no story at all.
Maimonides says the list proves the journey was real: anyone could see these were remote, barren places where people could only have survived by miracle. Rashi offers a parable instead.
A king's son fell ill, and the king took him on a long journey to a distant place to be healed.

teach.h: RASHI: HERE YOU HAD A HEADACHE.
teach.b: On the way home, the father pointed out every spot they passed: here we slept; here we were cold; here you had a headache. So too, Rashi says, God recounts to Israel all the places along the way. A very tender picture.

Not a map for travelers, but a parent's memory of a hard trip. Every stop is held in mind, including the ones where the child was miserable. In this reading the list says: the forgettable places counted too.
The people were carried through each one.

how: Masei, the last portion of Numbers, is read in midsummer, often together with Matot, and the list of journeys is chanted in full in synagogue, every station named.

o: the place where the water was bitter to drink
the journeys of: the portion that lists every camp

games.q: what's inside the list — tap the pairs.
p: a father recalling a sick son's trip

s: every station in the list comes with a story

games.q: you're writing down the history of a forty-year journey. most of the campsites were places where nothing happened. what do you do with them?
games.why: the Torah names every one, forty-two in tradition's count, even the stops with no story at all.

practice: Starting from your childhood home, or from ten years ago, name the places you've lived, worked, stayed or waited, one by one, without skipping the in-between ones.
At each, notice one thing: here I was lonely; here I learned something; here someone helped me.

wordCard.voice: Masei. The journeys of. And this week: morning and evening, keeping your word, a hard war, children first, standing with others, being clear before all, and now every stop named.

orig.note: Hebrew: the journeys of, from the opening words of Numbers 33.

carryVoice: Your line: every stop counts. Even the ones on the list with no story. Day four hundred seventy-six, done.
